readings.c1s1:
¶
'''breast-line''' (brest′līn), ''n.'' A rope used to unite the pontoons of a floating bridge.

'''breast-molding''' (brest′mōl″ding), ''n.'' '''1.''' The molding on a window-sill.—'''2.''' Paneling beneath a window.

'''breast-pain''' (brest′pān), ''n.'' A distemper in horses, indicated by stiffness and staggering of the fore legs, and inability to bow the head to the ground.

'''breast-pang''' (brest′pang), ''n.'' Angina pectoris. See ''angina.'' [Rare.]

'''breastpin''' (brest′pin), ''n.'' A pin worn on the breast for a fastening or for ornament; a brooch; a scarf-pin.

'''breastplate''' (brest′plāt), ''n.'' [ME. ''brestplate''; < ''breast'' + ''plate.''] '''1.''' A square ornament worn by the Jewish high priest, consisting of the same textile fabric as the ephod, and bearing twelve precious stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, set in gold. {{smaller|The breastplate was hung by chains of gold to that part of the ephod which was on the shoulder, and the lower side was secured to the girdle by blue laces; for this purpose four}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''breast-plow''' (brest′plou), ''n.'' A kind of spade with a cross-bar against which the breast is pressed to propel it, for cutting and paring turf.

'''breast-pump''' (brest′pump), ''n.'' A small suction apparatus for drawing milk from the breast.

'''breast-rail''' (brest′rāl), ''n.'' The upper rail of a balcony or of a breastwork on the quarter-deck of a ship.

'''breast-rope†''' (brest′rōp), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', an old term for ''parrel-rope.'' See ''breast-band'', 1.

'''breast-strap''' (brest′strap), ''n.'' A strap used to support the neck-yoke of a carriage-harness, and connected with the hames or collar.—{{smaller|'''Breast-strap slide''', an iron loop sliding on the breast-strap and taking the wear of the ring on the end of the neck-yoke.}}

'''breast-summer''', ''n.'' See ''brest-summer.''

'''breast-wall''' (brest′wâl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A retaining wall at the foot of a slope.—'''2.''' A wall built breast-high.

'''breastweed''' (brest′wēd), ''n.'' A name given to the lizard’s-tail of the United States, ''Saururus cernuus'', from its use as a remedy in mammary inflammation, etc.

'''breast-wheel''' (brest′hwēl), ''n.'' A water-wheel

water is admitted at any point from about the plane of the axle to 45° or more above it. {{smaller|The water is confined to the floats by a breasting of planks or masonry, almost touching the periphery of the wheel and extending from the bottom of the sluice to near the lowest point of the wheel. If the water is admitted to the wheel at a point very near its summit and on the same side as the sluice, it is called a ''pitch-back wheel.''}}

'''breast-wood''' (brest′wu̇d), ''n.'' In ''hort.'', the shoots of fruit-trees which grow out from the front of the branches trained on espaliers or against walls.

'''breastwork''' (brest′wėrk), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''fort.'', a hastily constructed work thrown up breast-high for defense.—'''2.''' ''Naut.'', a sort of balustrade of rails or moldings which terminates the quarter-deck and poop at the fore ends, and also incloses the forecastle both before and behind.—'''3.''' The parapet of a building.

'''breat''' (brēt), ''n.'' [Another form of ''bret'', ''brit'', q. v.] A local English name of the turbot.

'''breath''' (breth), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''breth'', < ME. ''breeth'', ''breth'', < AS. ''brǣth'', breath, odor; cf. OHG. ''brādam'', MHG. ''bradem'', G. ''brodem'', ''broden'', steam, vapor, exhalation; perhaps connected with AS. ''brǣdan'' = OHG. ''brātan'', MHG. ''brāten'', G. ''braten'', roast, broil (see ''brawn''), and with Gr. πρήθειν, burn, blow. The vowel in ''breath'', orig. long, has become short, while remaining long in the verb ''breathe''.] '''1†.''' Vapor; steam; exhalation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then schalle thou caste
Into the pot and cover in hast,
And loke no ''brethe'' ther passe out.</poem>
{{right|''Liber Cure Cocorum'', p. 19.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''8.''' A gentle exercise, causing a quicker respiration. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But, for your health and your digestion sake,
An after-dinner’s ''breath.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 3.}}}}

'''9.''' A respiratory movement, as of free air; a blowing.
{{smaller block|<poem>Calm and unruffled as a summer’s sea,
When not a ''breath'' of wind flies o’er its surface.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 4.}}}}

'''10.''' Spoken words; speech. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Art thou — thou — the slave that with thy ''breath'' hast kill’d
Mine innocent child?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 1.}}
<poem>I will stand,
Like the earth’s center, unmoved.—Lords, your ''breath''
Must finish these divisions.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v. 1.}}}}

'''11.''' A mere word; a trivial circumstance; a thing without substance; a trifle.
{{smaller block|<poem>A dream, a ''breath'', a froth of fleeting joy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 212.}}
<poem>A ''breath'' can make them, as a ''breath'' has made.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 54.}}}}

'''12.''' An odorous exhalation.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''breath''
Of the fading edges of box beneath.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Song.}}}}

'''13.''' In ''philol.'', a breathing; aspiration; aspirate sound.
{{smaller block|Even in the latest Semitic alphabets the ''breaths'' and semi-consonants of the primitive Semitic alphabet have retained their original character.
{{right|''Isaac Taylor'', The Alphabet, I. 184.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|breast-line|672|breathe}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''breast-line''' (brest′līn), ''n.'' A rope used to unite the pontoons of a floating bridge.

'''breast-molding''' (brest′mōl″ding), ''n.'' '''1.''' The molding on a window-sill.—'''2.''' Paneling beneath a window.

'''breast-pain''' (brest′pān), ''n.'' A distemper in horses, indicated by stiffness and staggering of the fore legs, and inability to bow the head to the ground.

'''breast-pang''' (brest′pang), ''n.'' Angina pectoris. See ''angina.'' [Rare.]

'''breastpin''' (brest′pin), ''n.'' A pin worn on the breast for a fastening or for ornament; a brooch; a scarf-pin.

'''breastplate''' (brest′plāt), ''n.''   [ME. ''brestplate''; < ''breast'' + ''plate.'']   '''1.''' A square ornament worn by the Jewish high priest, consisting of the same textile fabric as the ephod, and bearing twelve precious stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, set in gold. {{smaller|The breastplate was hung by chains of gold to that part of the ephod which was on the shoulder, and the lower side was secured to the girdle by blue laces; for this purpose four}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0698 c1f1.png|width=219px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Breastplate, 16th century; steel ornamented with gilding, and bearing a coat of arms on the breast. (From “L’Art pour Tous.”)}}}} {{smaller|rings of gold were secured to the four corners. It was also called the ''breastplate of judgment'', because it contained the Urim and the Thummim.}} '''2.''' The armor for the front of the body, when made in one piece reaching from the waist to about the collar-bone. {{smaller|It was not introduced until a very late period in the history of armor, and was not common until the early years of the sixteenth century, when armor for the limbs was being abandoned. See ''back and breast'' (under ''back''<sup>1</sup>), ''corselet'', and ''cuirass''.}}

'''3.''' A strap that runs across a horse’s breast.—'''4.''' A plate or piece which receives the butt-end of a boring-tool, and is held against the breast when the tool is in use. Also called ''conscience'' and ''palette''.—'''5.''' The sternum or central piece on the lower side of the cephalothorax of a spider, between the bases of the legs.—'''6.''' The lower shell or plastron of a tortoise.   ''Darwin.''

'''breast-plow''' (brest′plou), ''n.'' A kind of spade with a cross-bar against which the breast is pressed to propel it, for cutting and paring turf.

'''breast-pump''' (brest′pump), ''n.'' A small suction apparatus for drawing milk from the breast.

'''breast-rail''' (brest′rāl), ''n.'' The upper rail of a balcony or of a breastwork on the quarter-deck of a ship.

'''breast-rope†''' (brest′rōp), ''n.''   ''Naut.'', an old term for ''parrel-rope.'' See ''breast-band'', 1.

'''breast-strap''' (brest′strap), ''n.'' A strap used to support the neck-yoke of a carriage-harness, and connected with the hames or collar.—{{smaller|'''Breast-strap slide''', an iron loop sliding on the breast-strap and taking the wear of the ring on the end of the neck-yoke.}}

'''breast-summer''', ''n.'' See ''brest-summer.''

'''breast-wall''' (brest′wâl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A retaining wall at the foot of a slope.—'''2.''' A wall built breast-high.

'''breastweed''' (brest′wēd), ''n.'' A name given to the lizard’s-tail of the United States, ''Saururus cernuus'', from its use as a remedy in mammary inflammation, etc.

'''breast-wheel''' (brest′hwēl), ''n.'' A water-wheel with radial floats or buckets, upon which the water is admitted at any point from about the plane of the axle to 45° or more above it. {{smaller|The water is confined to the floats by a breasting of planks or masonry, almost touching the periphery of the wheel and extending from the bottom of the sluice to near the lowest point of the wheel. If the water is admitted to the wheel at a point very near its summit and on the same side as the sluice, it is called a ''pitch-back wheel.''}}

[[File:century v01 p0698 c1f2.png|center|239px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Breast-wheel.}}}}

'''breast-wood''' (brest′wu̇d), ''n.'' In ''hort.'', the shoots of fruit-trees which grow out from the front of the branches trained on espaliers or against walls.

'''breastwork''' (brest′wėrk), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''fort.'', a hastily constructed work thrown up breast-high for defense.—'''2.''' ''Naut.'', a sort of balustrade of rails or moldings which terminates the quarter-deck and poop at the fore ends, and also incloses the forecastle both before and behind.—'''3.''' The parapet of a building.

'''breat''' (brēt), ''n.''   [Another form of ''bret'', ''brit'', q. v.]   A local English name of the turbot.

'''breath''' (breth), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''breth'', < ME. ''breeth'', ''breth'', < AS. ''brǣth'', breath, odor; cf. OHG. ''brādam'', MHG. ''bradem'', G. ''brodem'', ''broden'', steam, vapor, exhalation; perhaps connected with AS. ''brǣdan'' = OHG. ''brātan'', MHG. ''brāten'', G. ''braten'', roast, broil (see ''brawn''), and with Gr. πρήθειν, burn, blow. The vowel in ''breath'', orig. long, has become short, while remaining long in the verb ''breathe''.]   '''1†.''' Vapor; steam; exhalation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then schalle thou caste
Into the pot and cover in hast,
And loke no ''brethe'' ther passe out.</poem>
{{right|''Liber Cure Cocorum'', p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>That is blode and fire and ''brethe'' of smoke.</poem>
{{right|''Hampole'', Prick of Conscience, l. 4727.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When bremly brened those besteȝ, & the ''brethe'' rysed,
The savour of his sacrafyse soȝt to hym euen
That all spedeȝ & spylleȝ.</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 509.}}}}
'''2.''' The air inhaled and exhaled in respiration.
{{smaller block|<poem>My ''breath'' to heaven like vapor goes:
May my soul follow soon!</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', St. Agnes’ Eve.}}}}
'''3.''' Ability to breathe; life as dependent on respiration.
{{smaller block|No man has more contempt than I of ''breath''.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''4.''' The state or power of breathing freely: as, to be out of ''breath;'' to be in ''breath.''
{{smaller block|<poem>The king shall drink to Hamlet’s better ''breath.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I lose my colour, I lose my ''breath.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Eleänore.}}}}
'''5.''' A single act of breathing; a respiration: as, he swears at every ''breath;'' to draw a full ''breath.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Between two ''breaths'' what crowded mysteries lie,—
The first short gasp, the last and long-drawn sigh!</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', A Rhymed Lesson.}}}}
Hence—'''6.''' The time of a single respiration; a single act; an instant.
{{smaller block|The historian makes two blunders in a ''breath.''
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sweet and bitter in a ''breath.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, iii.}}}}
'''7.''' Respite; pause; time to breathe.
{{smaller block|<poem>Give me some little ''breath'', some pause.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 2.}}}}

'''8.''' A gentle exercise, causing a quicker respiration. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But, for your health and your digestion sake,
An after-dinner’s ''breath.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 3.}}}}

'''9.''' A respiratory movement, as of free air; a blowing.
{{smaller block|<poem>Calm and unruffled as a summer’s sea,
When not a ''breath'' of wind flies o’er its surface.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 4.}}}}

'''10.''' Spoken words; speech. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Art thou — thou — the slave that with thy ''breath'' hast kill’d
Mine innocent child?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will stand,
Like the earth’s center, unmoved.—Lords, your ''breath''
Must finish these divisions.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v. 1.}}}}

'''11.''' A mere word; a trivial circumstance; a thing without substance; a trifle.
{{smaller block|<poem>A dream, a ''breath'', a froth of fleeting joy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 212.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''breath'' can make them, as a ''breath'' has made.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 54.}}}}

'''12.''' An odorous exhalation.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''breath''
Of the fading edges of box beneath.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Song.}}}}

'''13.''' In ''philol.'', a breathing; aspiration; aspirate sound.
{{smaller block|Even in the latest Semitic alphabets the ''breaths'' and semi-consonants of the primitive Semitic alphabet have retained their original character.
{{right|''Isaac Taylor'', The Alphabet, I. 184.}}}} '''14.''' Opinion; sentiments: as, I would fain hear his ''breath'' on this matter.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.] {{smaller|—'''Breath of the nostrils,''' in the Bible, vital breath (see Gen. ii. 7); hence, anything essential to the existence of a person or an institution; the inspiring cause of anything, or that which sustains it.}}
{{smaller block|No institutions spring up in such countries except those which the prince founds, and he may be truly said to be the ''breath of'' their ''nostrils.'' {{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''Out of breath,''' breathless; short of breath.}}
{{smaller block|Too much breathing put him ''out of breath.''
{{right|''Milton,'' Ep. Hobson, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To gather breath.''' See ''gather.''—'''To get one’s second breath,''' to recover the free use of the lungs after the first exhaustion incident to running, rowing, etc. [Colloq.]—'''Under the breath,''' in a whisper.—'''With bated breath.''' See ''bate''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''breathable''' (brē′ᴛʜa̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''breathe'' + ''-able.'']   Capable of being breathed; respirable.

'''breathableness''' (brē′ᴛʜa̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being breathable.

'''breathe''' (brēᴛʜ), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''breathed,'' ppr. ''breathing.''   [< ME. ''brethen,'' breathe, blow, exhale odor, < ''breth,'' breath: see ''breath.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To draw air into and expel it from the lungs; respire; figuratively, to live.
{{smaller block|When he ''breathed'' he was a man. ''Shak.,'' L. L. L., v. 2.
<poem>Where, in the vast world,
Doth that man ''breathe,'' that can so much command
His blood and his affection?</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Every Man out of his Humour, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I did
God’s bidding and man’s duty, so, ''breathe'' free.</poem>
{{right|''Browning,'' Ring and Book, I. 253.}}}}
'''2.''' To make a single respiration.
{{smaller block|Before you can say, Come, and Go, And ''breathe'' twice. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To take breath; rest from action.
{{smaller block|''Breathe'' awhile, and then to ’t again.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Well, let this ''breathe'' a while.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, v. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' To pass, as air; blow: as, “when winds ''breathe'' sweet,” ''Shak.'', Lover’s Compl., l. 103.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh, ''breathe'' upon thy ruined vineyard still;
Though like the dead it long unmoved has lain.</poem>
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 88.}}}}
'''5.''' To give utterance to disparaging or calumnious remarks; make insinuations: with ''upon.''
{{smaller block|You must seem to take as unpardonable offence, as if he had torn your mistress’s colours, or ''breathed upon'' her picture.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, i. 1.}}}}
'''6.''' To exhale, as an odor; emanate.
{{smaller block|And all Arabia ''breathes'' from yonder box.
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., i. 134.}}}}
'''7.''' Figuratively, of inanimate things, to be instinct; be alive.
{{smaller block|The staircase in fresco by Sir James Thornhill ''breathed'' with the loves and wars of gods and heroes.
{{right|''Disraeli.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To inhale and exhale in respiration: as, to ''breathe'' vitiated air.—'''2.''' To inject by breathing; infuse: with ''into:'' as, “to ''breathe'' life ''into'' a stone,” ''Shak.'', All’s Well, ii. 1.
{{smaller block|And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and ''breathed into'' his nostrils the breath of life. Gen. ii. 7.
<poem>Where faith made whole with deed
''Breathes'' its awakening breath
''Into'' the lifeless creed.
{{right|''Lowell'', Comm. Ode.</poem>}}}}
'''3.''' To exhale; send out as breath; express; manifest. {{smaller block|<poem>Can any mortal mixture of earth’s mould
''Breathe'' such divine, enchanting ravishment?</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 245.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [the Indians] entered . . . into an agreement to twenty-nine rules, all ''breathing'' a desire to conform themselves to English customs.
{{right|''Emerson'', Historical Discourse at Concord.}}}}
'''4.''' To exercise; keep in breath.
{{smaller block|Methinks . . . every man should beat thee; I think thou wast created for men to ''breathe'' themselves upon thee.
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|I’ll send for one of these fencers, and he shall ''breathe'' you, by my direction.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, i. 4.}}}}
'''5.''' To inspire or blow into; cause to sound by breathing.
{{smaller block|They ''breathe'' the flute or strike the vocal wire.
{{right|''Prior.''}}}}
'''6.''' To utter; speak; whisper.
{{smaller block|<poem>Or let the church, our mother, ''breathe'' her curse.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus ''breathes'' she forth her spite.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 762.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>That ''breathe'' a thousand tender vows.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xx.}}}}
'''7.''' To suffer to rest or recover breath.
{{smaller block|<poem>He ''breath’d'' his sword, and rested him till day.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xi. 47.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A moment now he slacked his speed,
A moment ''breathed'' his panting steed.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., i.}}}}
'''8.''' To open and bleed (a vein).
{{smaller block|Every village barber who ''breathed'' a vein.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XI. 503.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
